description:
I'm a software engineering student from Kyrgyzstan with a strong interest in technology, data analysis, AI, and solving real-world problems through innovative solutions. I enjoy exploring new technologies, learning new skills, and turning ideas into practical projects.

You don't have to be an expert in everything. I'm looking for motivated people with complementary skills, a willingness to learn, and a shared ambition to create something impactful.
summary:
AgroShift helps small farms in Kyrgyzstan’s Chüy Valley plan their season. Every spring a farmer has to decide what to plant, and nobody can tell him whether the canal will give enough water that year. A dry year can cost him the harvest, and with it the money his family needs to get through the autumn.

We took 30 years of NASA POWER climate data (temperature, solar radiation, humidity, wind and rainfall) and used the FAO-56 method to estimate how much water crops use. For every 10-day period we calculate how much water a field needs and compare it with what the canal schedule actually delivers. Then we run the farmer’s plan through each of the last 30 years, along with a few other options, and count how often each one ends with too little water or too little money. There’s also a stress test, so the farmer can check something like “what if July water drops by 20% and feed costs go up by 40%?”

Water user associations get a view of the whole canal. AgroShift adds up demand from all the farms on it and suggests a shared sowing and irrigation schedule, so that not everyone needs water in the same week. In our demo this cut the peak shortage by about 40%.

Our idea is that a farmer shouldn’t have to understand climate data to benefit from it. He should simply see what to plant, when to irrigate and how much he’s risking.
details:
What it does

AgroShift helps small farmers and water user associations in Kyrgyzstan’s Chüy Valley plan the season around the water they will actually get. A farmer enters his fields, crops, livestock, cash and the canal turn schedule. AgroShift then looks at the plan in three ways:

  1. Field: does each crop get enough water in every 10-day period?
  2. Farm: do money and feed last through every month?
  3. Shared canal: what happens when all the neighbours need water at the same time?

How it works

  • For each field we take 30 years of daily NASA POWER weather data for its grid cell: temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation and precipitation.
  • We calculate reference evapotranspiration with the FAO-56 Penman–Monteith method, then crop water needs for each growth stage. On top of that we run a daily soil water balance that accounts for canal turns and water lost in the channels.
  • We use the FAO-33 yield response method to estimate how much yield a farmer loses when water runs short. A monthly cash flow and feed balance model then converts that into money.
  • We treat each of the 30 years as a separate test of the plan. So the farmer gets a concrete number, like “your plan runs out of cash in 5 of 30 years”, which is more useful than a general drought warning.
  • The optimizer runs every allowed crop combination through all 30 years. For the demo farm that’s 80 options. It shows the best one for each goal (higher income, less water, or getting through a bad year) next to the farmer’s own plan.
  • The stress test lets you cut water in chosen months or add heat, higher feed prices or a late payment. It shows the loss in som and what change would win it back.
  • For a whole canal, AgroShift adds up demand from all farms and finds the 10-day periods where demand peaks. It then suggests moving sowing dates in a way that stays fair to everyone. Each farm sees only its own suggestion and never its neighbours’ finances. In our demo with 20 farms, peak demand went down by 16%.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Farmers can see before planting which month their plan fails in and how much it would cost to adjust.
  • Water user associations get a way to plan scarce canal water, so it isn’t just whoever comes first.
  • For the Ministry of Agriculture, this is a practical way to get satellite data into everyday farm decisions. Our team captain works there as a business analyst, and he often sees this kind of data end up only on a map or in a report.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy/GeoAlchemy2, Alembic, PostgreSQL 16 + PostGIS, NumPy, Parquet climate snapshots
  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, MapLibre GL, ECharts
  • Infrastructure and quality: Docker Compose, pytest (199 tests), Ruff, GitHub with dev/main branches
  • Data: NASA POWER (agroclimatology), FAO-56 and FAO-33 methods. Next we plan to add GPM IMERG, MODIS snow cover and HLS.

What makes it creative

  • We started from the farmer’s decision, not from a map. The result tells him what to plant and what risk comes with it.
  • We use 30 years of NASA history as 30 possible versions of the coming season.
  • The plan is checked at three connected levels: field, farm and canal. Most tools we looked at only work at the field level.
  • We try to be clear about what we don’t know. Every number shows where it came from and how complete the data is, and anything we had to guess is marked as an estimate.

Factors we considered

  • Missing data: many farms keep no records for individual fields, so we use reference values and show their ranges.
  • Fairness and privacy between neighbours on the same canal.
  • Language: the interface works in Kyrgyz, Russian and English.
  • Validation: we haven’t done it yet. For the 2027 season we plan a pilot on one canal, where we’ll compare NASA POWER with local weather stations and check the yield and cash models with agronomists and farmers.
  • Demo data: in this prototype the farm finances and the canal are made up for the demo, and the app marks them as demo data.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (LaRC)  Daily weather data for any coordinates since 1981: temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation, precipitation. We use it to calculate crop water demand (evapotranspiration) and to build a 30-year history for estimating how often dry years occur.
NASA POWER API  Open REST interface with no API key required. We used it to download weather snapshots for three pilot points in the Chuy region: Sokuluk, Kant, and Kara-Balta.
